# The Two-Queue Scheduler and Deadlock Avoidance {#sec-two-queue-scheduler}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
This chapter has been drafted end-to-end against NebulaStream commit
`cd3ef68c73`. It is the smoke-test chapter for the book — the first one
written, used to validate voice and tooling. Maintainer review pending.
:::

A stream processing engine is, at its heart, a machine for moving
tuples between stateful operators. The scheduler decides which operator
runs next and on which worker thread. Get it wrong and the engine
either starves under load, livelocks under pressure, or — most
embarrassingly — deadlocks itself into a frozen process that has to be
killed and restarted.

In this chapter we open up NebulaStream's scheduler. The structure we
will examine is, in code, fewer than two hundred lines. The reasons it
exists, the bugs that pushed it to its current shape, and the trade-offs
it embodies — those take the rest of the chapter.

We will not start with the solution. We will start with the bug.

---

## 15.1 The problem: a bounded queue and two ways to deadlock {#sec-bounded-queue-problem}

Most production stream engines distribute work across a pool of worker
threads using a shared task queue. Worker threads dequeue tasks, do
some work, and emit follow-up tasks back to the queue. Sources also
emit tasks: when a CSV file source reads a fresh batch of bytes and
parses it into a `TupleBuffer`, it emits a task instructing some
downstream pipeline to consume that buffer.

In an idealised version of this design, the queue is unbounded. A task
is always accepted, the producer never has to wait, and you only need
to decide on dequeue order. In practice, an unbounded queue is a way
to crash later. Memory is finite; if a fast source can permanently
out-produce the workers, the queue grows without bound and the process
exhausts its address space. The fix, almost reflexively, is to make
the queue bounded.

Then you have a different problem.

A bounded queue, by definition, can be full. If a producer tries to
write to a full queue, you have three choices: drop the task, return
an error, or block the producer until space is available. Stream
engines almost always choose to block — dropping or erroring would
break the engine's processing guarantees. Blocking the producer is
called *backpressure* and it is the right answer. It is also the answer
that introduces deadlocks.

There are two distinct ways the engine can deadlock against its own
bounded queue. NebulaStream's design document for the query engine
calls them P1 and P2 [@nes-task-queue-doc]. We will use the same
labels.

**P1 — worker-emission deadlock.** A worker thread holding a task
attempts to emit a follow-up task. The queue is full. The thread
blocks waiting for capacity. But capacity will only become available
when *some other worker thread* dequeues a task, finishes it, and
*emits its own follow-up*. If every worker is in the same
emit-and-block state, no worker dequeues. The system deadlocks.

This is not a hypothetical scenario. It is what happens during a hash
join probe, where each input tuple may produce many output tuples; or
during a window trigger, where firing a window emits a fan-out of
downstream work. In both cases, a single dequeued task can produce
many emitted tasks, and the queue can fill from the inside out.

**P2 — source-flooding deadlock.** Sources are not workers. A source
thread does not dequeue tasks; it only emits them. If the source is
faster than the workers — say, a high-rate sensor or a Kafka topic
being replayed at full speed — the source can fill the queue with
unprocessed tuples faster than the workers drain it. Once the queue is
full, the source blocks; once the source blocks, no new work enters;
the workers drain the queue and idle. Then the source unblocks and the
cycle resumes. This is not a deadlock in the strict sense (the system
makes progress eventually) but it has two ugly consequences. First,
the workers cycle between full saturation and complete idleness. The
throughput of the system is dictated by the queue size and not by the
hardware. Second — more dangerously — if the worker emits a follow-up
task while the queue is saturated by source-emitted tasks, the worker
also blocks. Now we are back in P1.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.1: P1 in a hash join probe"}
Consider a hash join with two input streams `R` and `S`. The build
side `R` has been hashed into an in-memory hash table. A `WorkTask`
arrives for `S`: process this 8 KiB batch of `S` tuples. The probe
finds matches for, on average, 1.7 tuples per input tuple, so the
batch produces a follow-up batch about 1.7× as large.

The worker dequeues the `S`-side `WorkTask`, performs the probe,
and now needs to emit a follow-up `WorkTask` for the next operator
downstream. If every worker thread is in this state — having just
dequeued an `S` task and trying to emit a probe-result task — and
the queue is full, no worker can emit and no worker can dequeue.
That is P1.
:::

The two problems sound similar but they have different fixes. We will
solve them separately.

---

## 15.2 Solving P1: do not block the worker on emit {#sec-solving-p1}

The cleanest fix to P1 is to ensure that *worker threads never block
on emit*. A worker thread that holds work must always be able to make
progress.

NebulaStream's published design document
[@nes-task-queue-doc, §Continuation] proposes a technique called
*continuation*. When a worker fails to write its follow-up task to the
queue, instead of blocking, the worker swaps: it stuffs its
unsubmittable task into a thread-local slot and pulls one task off the
queue to work on next. The next time the worker comes back to its
slot, the queue may have drained enough to accept the swapped task.

Continuation is elegant. It also has a subtle trap, identified in the
same design document: some tasks cannot make progress on their own. A
`PendingPipelineStop` task — which we will examine in detail in
@sec-pending-pipeline-stop — checks whether a pipeline still has
references and, if so, *re-emits itself*. If continuation forced the
worker to take this task off the queue and immediately swap it back,
the worker would loop without making progress.

The published design proposes a workaround: instead of swapping, the
worker takes one task off the queue, *replaces* its own task with that
one, and works on the replacement. The original task gets put back at
the end of the queue.

::: {.callout-warning title="Caveat: the live code uses a different fix"}
The design document was written when the internal queue was bounded.
The current implementation uses an *unbounded* internal queue. The
worker-emit path therefore cannot fail at all; continuation is no
longer needed for P1.

You can verify this directly. Open
`/Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/nes-query-engine/TaskQueue.hpp`
and observe that the internal queue is declared as
`folly::UMPMCQueue<TaskType, true>` — the U is for unbounded — while
only the admission queue is `folly::MPMCQueue<TaskType>`. The method
`addInternalTaskNonBlocking` carries this guarantee in its name, and
its body has no failure path:

```cpp
template <typename T = TaskType>
void addInternalTaskNonBlocking(T&& task)
{
    /// The order of operation upholds the invariant. internal is
    /// unbounded which makes this write always succeed (unless oom)
    internal.enqueue(std::forward<T>(task));
    tasksAvailable.release();
}
```

This is the engine's actual P1 fix as of `cd3ef68c73`: don't bound
the queue worker threads write to. We will use this as our reference
throughout the chapter and note where the design document's
continuation scheme would still be needed if a future change made the
internal queue bounded again.
:::

The choice between an unbounded internal queue and a bounded queue
plus continuation is a real engineering trade-off, not a settled
matter.

The unbounded approach buys simplicity. Worker code never needs to
handle a write failure; emission is a trivial enqueue. It also buys
correctness for the `PendingPipelineStop` scenario: a self-emitting
task can simply be appended without any concern about replacing a
worker's current task.

The cost is that the engine no longer has a hard backpressure surface
on the worker side. If a query produces a pathological amount of
internal fan-out — imagine a many-to-many join with no selectivity —
the internal queue can grow until it crashes the process. In practice
this is bounded by other constraints: the number of `TupleBuffer`s in
the pool (we will see why in [Chapter 16](16-stateful-operators.qmd)), the
selectivity of upstream operators, the rate at which sources can be
admitted (the next section). NebulaStream's authors have decided that
those constraints are sufficient. Other engines have decided
differently; we will see Flink's choice in @sec-reading-order's
sidebar.

---

## 15.3 Solving P2: a separate admission queue {#sec-solving-p2}

P2 — source-flooding — needs a different fix because it has a
different cause. The issue is not that producers can block; it is
that *some kinds of producers should be allowed to block, and others
should not*. Sources can wait. Worker threads cannot.

NebulaStream's solution is to physically separate the two kinds of
producers into two queues:

- **`internal`** — the unbounded queue that worker threads emit into.
  Always accepts a write; never blocks.
- **`admission`** — a bounded queue that sources, query starts, and
  query stops emit into. Blocks the producer when full.

Worker threads dequeue from a logical merger of both: the internal
queue is preferred, the admission queue is fallback. From the worker's
point of view, there is just one source of work; from the producer's
point of view, there are two clearly distinct paths with different
blocking semantics.

The implementation is in `nes-query-engine/TaskQueue.hpp`. Two folly
queues, one semaphore, three public methods. The whole file is 124
lines.

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/TaskQueue.hpp:34-44
template <typename TaskType>
class TaskQueue
{
    folly::UMPMCQueue<TaskType, true> internal;
    folly::MPMCQueue<TaskType> admission;

    /// INVARIANT: internal.size() + admission.size() >= tasksAvailable
    std::counting_semaphore<> tasksAvailable{0};
    // ...
};
```

The line `INVARIANT: internal.size() + admission.size() >=
tasksAvailable` is the heart of the design. We will return to it in
@sec-semaphore-invariant.

Three public write/read methods complete the interface:

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/TaskQueue.hpp:71-94
template <typename T = TaskType>
bool addAdmissionTaskBlocking(const std::stop_token& stoken, T&& task);

template <typename T = TaskType>
void addInternalTaskNonBlocking(T&& task);

std::optional<TaskType> getNextTaskBlocking(const std::stop_token& stoken);
```

Three methods, three intents. The method names carry the semantics:
admission is blocking, internal is non-blocking, dequeue is blocking
with cancellation. There is also a non-blocking dequeue
(`getNextTaskNonBlocking`) which we will not need in this chapter.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.2: P2 in a fast source"}
A `TCPSource` is connected to a sensor producing a million events
per second. Each batch of ten thousand events becomes one
`WorkTask` written into the admission queue. The admission queue
is sized at, say, four hundred slots.

If the workers can process eight hundred batches per second, the
queue fills in half a second. The source thread blocks on
`addAdmissionTaskBlocking`. Meanwhile, the workers continue to
drain — and crucially, when a worker emits a follow-up task into
the *internal* queue, that emission still succeeds, because the
internal queue is unbounded.

The source's blocking has, by design, no effect on worker progress.
The fast sensor experiences backpressure (its TCP buffer fills, its
TCP window shrinks, the upstream sensor learns to slow down) but
the engine is not deadlocked. P2 is solved.
:::

---

## 15.4 Reading order: who wins the dequeue race {#sec-reading-order}

We have two queues. A worker thread asks for the next task. Which
queue do we read from?

The simple rule: prefer internal, fall back to admission.

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/TaskQueue.hpp:47-63
TaskType readElementAssumingItExists()
{
    TaskType task;
    /// The semaphore guarantees that there is at least one element in
    /// either one of the queues.
    if (internal.try_dequeue(task))
    {
        return task;
    }

    /// However, the MPMC `read` can spuriously fail under high contention,
    /// the alternative `readIfNotEmpty` does not but is significantly
    /// slower.
    while (!admission.read(task)) [[unlikely]]
    {
    }

    return task;
}
```

The internal queue is checked first because it represents *work
already accepted into the engine*. Tuples currently passing between
operators have priority over new tuples knocking at the door. This is
the heart of the deadlock avoidance: a worker that cannot emit is, by
construction, impossible (the internal queue is unbounded), but if it
could be impossible, we would still want this read order, because it
ensures that work-in-progress drains before new work is admitted.

Said differently: this discipline gives priority to old work. If the
admission queue is overwhelmed, sources will block. If the internal
queue is overwhelmed, the workers will eventually drain it because
nothing fights them for it.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how this differs in Flink"}
Apache Flink uses a different model. Each operator has a fixed pool
of network buffers (`NetworkBufferPool`) [@flink-buffers]. When an
upstream operator emits a record, it must obtain a buffer; if no
buffers are available, it blocks. There is no separate
"admission" queue: backpressure travels through the operator chain
itself, and the source naturally blocks because everything between
it and the source has filled up.

Flink's approach has the virtue of fine-grained, per-pipeline
backpressure (one slow operator backpressures only its predecessors)
but is intrinsically more complex: every operator has a buffer
budget, every emit can block, every operator must be able to
correctly handle blocking on emit.

NebulaStream's two-queue model is coarser. Backpressure is global to
the engine, not per-operator. The simplification is the point.
:::

There is one subtle implementation note in `readElementAssumingItExists`
that deserves attention: the `while` loop on `admission.read`. The
loop is annotated `[[unlikely]]` and a comment explains why: the
folly `MPMCQueue::read` method can spuriously fail under high
contention even when the queue is non-empty. The semaphore *promises*
us a task is available; the queue, briefly, lies about it. The
alternative `readIfNotEmpty` does not lie but is — the comment tells
us — significantly slower.

This is a textbook example of the kind of trade-off you do not see
unless you read the actual code. A design document, when summarising,
will say "we read from the queue." The implementation says "we
sometimes spin on a contended dequeue because the alternative is too
slow." Both are true; the second is more useful.

---

## 15.5 The semaphore invariant {#sec-semaphore-invariant}

The invariant printed in the comment on line 40 is doing the heavy
lifting:

> `INVARIANT: internal.size() + admission.size() >= tasksAvailable`

The sum of the two queue sizes is at least equal to the semaphore
counter. The semaphore counter is the engine's notion of "how many
tasks are available right now." That count must never exceed the real
number of tasks, or a worker thread will be told that work exists when
in fact it does not, and the worker will spin or fail.

The invariant is upheld by carefully ordering the operations on each
write path. Both `addAdmissionTaskBlocking` and `addInternalTaskNonBlocking`
release the semaphore *only after* the task has actually been enqueued.
On the dequeue side, the worker first acquires the semaphore (blocking
if the count is zero) and only then attempts to read the task. The
acquire is the worker's promise that a task exists. The semaphore is
the only synchronisation between writer and reader visible to the
queue's API.

This is the kind of invariant that, on paper, is a single line. In a
production system, it is tested against thousands of randomised
producer/consumer interleavings. NebulaStream's
`tests/TaskQueueTest.cpp` exercises this directly with a multi-producer,
multi-consumer fuzzer that reasons about the order of writes vs. reads
to expose any window in which the invariant could be violated.

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 15.1: run the queue's own tests"}
Run the `TaskQueue` unit tests:

```shell
ctest --test-dir cmake-build-debug -R "TaskQueueTest" --output-on-failure
```

Open `nes-query-engine/tests/TaskQueueTest.cpp` and identify the
`Task` type the test uses (a `std::tuple<int, int,
std::array<std::byte, 142>>`). Why 142? Compare to the real
`sizeof(NES::Task)` and explain the comment "142 is roughly the
current task size." Does the queue's behaviour change if the task is
much larger?
:::

## 15.6 The Task variant: not all tasks are workunits {#sec-task-variant}

We have been speaking as if "task" meant only "process this batch of
tuples." It does not. The task type is a `std::variant` of eight
distinct task kinds, defined in `nes-query-engine/Task.hpp:195-203`:

```cpp
using Task = std::variant<
    WorkTask,
    StopQueryTask,
    StartQueryTask,
    FailSourceTask,
    StopSourceTask,
    PendingPipelineStopTask,
    StopPipelineTask,
    StartPipelineTask>;
```

`WorkTask` is the one we have been discussing: process tuples in a
specific buffer through a specific pipeline node. The other seven
control the *lifecycle* of queries, sources and pipelines. They flow
through the same queue infrastructure as data because the engine has
chosen to model "stop this pipeline" and "process this tuple" as the
same kind of event: a thing the worker thread does next.

The choice is unusual. Many engines model lifecycle changes as
out-of-band signals — a separate control plane, sometimes a separate
thread. NebulaStream multiplexes them onto the worker queue. The
benefit is that lifecycle changes are naturally serialised against
data: a `StopQueryTask` cannot accidentally race with the data it is
trying to stop, because it is processed by a worker between two data
tasks. The cost is that lifecycle work blocks behind data work, and
the engine has to be careful to ensure lifecycle work is not starved.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.3: a query stop is just another task"}
A user submits `STOP QUERY 42`. The frontend translates this into
a `StopQueryTask` and writes it to the admission queue. The
admission queue is currently full of `WorkTask`s for query 42. The
`StopQueryTask` waits.

A worker thread picks up the next admitted task — say, a `WorkTask`
for query 42. It processes the tuples. Now the worker dequeues
again, finds the `StopQueryTask`, and runs it: the query catalog is
consulted, the pipelines are torn down, the sources are signalled
to stop.

The query stop is naturally serialised behind the work that was
already in flight. There is no race between "process tuple 9 in
query 42" and "stop query 42" because they happen on the same
worker thread, in queue order.
:::

The most interesting member of the variant — the one that motivates
the rest of this chapter — is `PendingPipelineStopTask`.

---

## 15.7 Pending pipeline stops: when even two queues are not enough {#sec-pending-pipeline-stop}

Stopping a pipeline gracefully means waiting until no task currently
references it. Tasks reference pipelines through a `weak_ptr`; the
pipeline node is `shared_ptr`-owned by the engine, with task-local
`weak_ptr` references. Until the last task referencing a pipeline has
run to completion, the pipeline cannot be torn down without risking
a use-after-free.

The engine therefore models graceful pipeline shutdown as a polling
task: a `PendingPipelineStopTask` that examines the pipeline's
reference count, and if any task is still referencing it, *re-emits
itself* to be checked again later.

This is the task type that broke the simple version of continuation.
A `PendingPipelineStopTask` cannot make progress on its own; it can
only make progress as other, unrelated tasks ahead of it in the queue
finish.

The current implementation handles this with a small backoff
mechanism. Look at `QueryEngine.cpp:600-625`:

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/QueryEngine.cpp:608-624
if (pendingPipelineStop.pipeline->pendingTasks > 0)
{
    ENGINE_LOG_TRACE(
        "Pipeline {}-{} is still active: {}. Seen for {}th time",
        pendingPipelineStop.queryId,
        pendingPipelineStop.pipeline->id,
        pendingPipelineStop.pipeline->pendingTasks,
        pendingPipelineStop.attempts);

    PendingPipelineStopTask repeatTask(
        pendingPipelineStop.queryId,
        pendingPipelineStop.pipeline,
        pendingPipelineStop.attempts + 1,
        std::move(pendingPipelineStop.callback));
    if (pendingPipelineStop.attempts >= PIPELINE_STOP_BACKOFF_THRESHOLD)
    {
        pool.delayedTaskSubmitter.submitTaskIn(
            std::move(repeatTask), PIPELINE_STOP_BACKOFF_INTERVAL);
    }
    else
    {
        pool.addInternalTask(std::move(repeatTask));
    }
    return false;
}
```

The pattern is: try the immediate re-enqueue twice; on the third
attempt, route through a `DelayedTaskSubmitter` that holds the task
for `PIPELINE_STOP_BACKOFF_INTERVAL` (25 ms, defined two screens up at
line 70) before re-introducing it. The constants are deliberately
small. This is not exponential backoff. It is a single hop from "try
again immediately" to "try again in 25 ms" — enough delay to let the
admission queue drain a few tasks but not enough to noticeably affect
shutdown latency.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.4: walking through a pipeline stop"}
A pipeline `P` has three in-flight `WorkTask`s. A `StopQueryTask`
for `P`'s query arrives; the engine processes it by emitting a
`PendingPipelineStopTask` for `P`.

The `PendingPipelineStopTask` is dequeued. Worker observes
`pipeline->pendingTasks == 3`, increments `attempts` to 1, and re-
emits the task to the internal queue. The task is now behind two
remaining `WorkTask`s.

Worker dequeues a `WorkTask`, processes it, decrements
`pendingTasks` to 2. Then dequeues the `PendingPipelineStopTask`
again. Sees 2 remaining, increments `attempts` to 2, re-emits.

Now `attempts == 2 == PIPELINE_STOP_BACKOFF_THRESHOLD`. The task is
routed through `DelayedTaskSubmitter` and held for 25 ms. During
that window, the two remaining `WorkTask`s drain. When the delayed
task is reinjected, `pendingTasks == 0`, the pipeline is torn down,
the callback fires.
:::

A natural question: why a backoff at all? Why not let the
`PendingPipelineStopTask` repeatedly re-enqueue itself until the
references drop to zero?

The answer is in the comment immediately above the threshold check
(`QueryEngine.cpp:614-615`):

> If we have seen this pipeline for the third time, we will add some
> work from the admission queue to the internal queue. We need to do
> this, as the pipeline might be stuck in a deadlock as it is waiting
> for data from a source which has not been moved into the internal
> queue.

A pipeline that is waiting for data from a source can only get that
data via the admission queue. If the worker keeps spinning on
`PendingPipelineStopTask` re-enqueues, no admission-queue task
will ever advance, because the internal queue keeps refilling itself
with the same self-emitting task. The 25 ms delay is not just polite;
it is correctness. It guarantees that the worker's gaze leaves the
internal queue long enough for a source-emitted task to be promoted.

This is a third deadlock possibility — a sub-case of P1 — that the
two-queue design alone does not solve. It needs the
`DelayedTaskSubmitter` as a dedicated escape hatch.

---

## 15.8 Cancellation as a first-class concern {#sec-cancellation}

The two queues block in different ways. The admission queue blocks
producers when it is full. The dequeue blocks consumers when both
queues are empty. Either blocking call must be cancellable — the
engine has to be able to shut down even if every queue is in a
pathological state.

NebulaStream uses C++20's `std::stop_token` for this, plumbed through
both blocking methods. Look at the dequeue path:

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/TaskQueue.hpp:100-111
std::optional<TaskType> getNextTaskBlocking(const std::stop_token& stoken)
{
    while (!tasksAvailable.try_acquire_for(StopTokenCheckInterval))
    {
        if (stoken.stop_requested())
        {
            return std::nullopt;
        }
    }

    return readElementAssumingItExists();
}
```

The semaphore is acquired *with a timeout* — `StopTokenCheckInterval`,
defined as 100 ms. Each timeout, the thread checks the stop token. If
shutdown has been requested, the method returns an empty optional and
the worker exits. Otherwise, it tries to acquire again.

The 100 ms interval is the maximum cancellation latency a worker
thread experiences when it is waiting for work. It is short enough
that a user-initiated shutdown feels instant. It is long enough that
the polling cost is invisible: ten checks per second per thread is
nothing.

The same pattern guards the producer side. `addAdmissionTaskBlocking`
loops `tryWriteUntil` with the same 100 ms interval, returning
`false` if the stop token fires before the write succeeds.

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/TaskQueue.hpp:71-85
template <typename T = TaskType>
bool addAdmissionTaskBlocking(const std::stop_token& stoken, T&& task)
{
    while (!stoken.stop_requested())
    {
        if (admission.tryWriteUntil(
                std::chrono::steady_clock::now() + StopTokenCheckInterval,
                std::forward<T>(task)))
        {
            tasksAvailable.release();
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}
```

There is one piece of nuance worth remarking on. The dequeue method's
documentation states: *"The method prioritizes reading over
cancellation. This implies, if a read is non-blocking, it succeeds
regardless of the state of the stop token."* That is, a worker that
finds work available will process it even during shutdown, rather than
exiting with the work unfinished. This is a design choice in favour of
draining over abandonment. It pairs naturally with the
`PendingPipelineStopTask` mechanism: shutdown processes shut down
gracefully through the same queue, alongside the data they are tearing
down.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: Spark Streaming and graceful stop"}
Spark Structured Streaming similarly distinguishes "stop now" from
"stop gracefully" via the `gracefulStop` parameter on
`StreamingQuery.stop()` [@spark-graceful-stop]. The mechanism differs
— Spark drains the current micro-batch and then halts — but the
underlying principle is the same: producers and consumers both need
a cooperative cancellation signal, and "drain in flight, then
exit" is almost always the right default.

NebulaStream's choice to model graceful stop as a first-class
`PendingPipelineStopTask` traveling through the worker queue (rather
than as out-of-band lifecycle state) makes the draining semantics
natural to enforce.
:::

---

## 15.9 Putting it together: the worker loop {#sec-worker-loop}

We have now seen all the pieces. Let us assemble them into a single
mental model of the worker loop.

![The worker thread loop. The wait at top is bounded by `StopTokenCheckInterval` (100 ms) so cancellation has bounded latency. Every code path eventually returns to the wait, except the `Worker exits` exit on shutdown.](../figures/tikz/ch15-worker-loop.svg){#fig-worker-loop width=90%}

Each loop iteration does at most one of: (a) acquire and process a
single task, (b) time out and check for shutdown. There is no
spinning, no polling, no busy work between tasks. The only place a
worker thread waits is on `tasksAvailable.try_acquire_for`, and that
wait is bounded by `StopTokenCheckInterval`.

Source threads and external producers run a parallel loop with a
different shape: they emit tasks via `addAdmissionTaskBlocking` and
their throughput is bounded by the admission queue's capacity.

The two loops meet at one point: the semaphore. The semaphore is the
only piece of synchronisation that workers and producers share. The
queues themselves are lock-free (folly's MPMC and UMPMC are both
implemented atop atomics, with no mutexes on the hot paths). The
combination — lock-free data structures synchronised by a counting
semaphore that doubles as a cancellation point — is what gives the
scheduler its blend of low overhead and clean shutdown semantics.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: Materialize and timely dataflow"}
Materialize is built on differential dataflow [@differential-dataflow],
which uses a fundamentally different scheduling model: a *frontier*
of timestamps that operators advance cooperatively, with no central
queue. Each worker thread owns a slice of the operator graph and
runs operators round-robin against their pending work.

Timely dataflow's strength is fine-grained progress reasoning;
NebulaStream's strength (with its central two-queue scheduler) is
operational simplicity. The two designs sit on opposite ends of the
"how distributed should the scheduler itself be" spectrum.
:::

---

## 15.10 What this design does not do {#sec-non-goals}

It is worth being explicit about what the two-queue scheduler does
*not* attempt.

**It does not prioritise tasks.** The design document is explicit on
this point [@nes-task-queue-doc, §Scope]: "It does not perform any
prioritization of tasks in terms of latency or throughput, but
prevents deadlocks." A latency-sensitive query and a throughput-
oriented query share the same queue and are processed in arrival
order. If a future version of the engine wants per-query scheduling
policies, the queue infrastructure will need to be replaced or
augmented; the current design is silent on the question.

**It does not implement work stealing in the strict sense.** Work
stealing, as in Cilk or Tokio's multi-threaded executor, gives each
worker a private deque and lets idle workers steal from busy ones'
deques. NebulaStream has a single shared queue (well, two), and
workers race to dequeue from it. The behaviour is similar — idle
workers always pick up available work — but the mechanism is
classical shared-queue work distribution, not work stealing.

**It does not model per-pipeline backpressure.** As we saw in the
Flink sidebar, some engines push backpressure through the operator
graph itself. NebulaStream's backpressure is global: when the
admission queue is full, *all* sources block, regardless of which
pipeline is the bottleneck. A slow downstream operator backpressures
fast upstream sources, but only because the workers are busy and
cannot drain fast enough — there is no targeted signal to throttle a
specific source. This is fine for the engine's current scale; if
NebulaStream grows to thousands of concurrent queries with very
heterogeneous resource needs, it will likely need a more discriminating
mechanism.

**It is per-worker, not cross-worker.** Each NebulaStream worker
has its own pair of queues and its own pool of worker threads.
In a distributed deployment (Chapter 19), task scheduling is
local to each worker; the network channels between workers are
the only inter-worker coordination, and they speak in
`TupleBuffer`s, not in `Task`s. Backpressure across workers
travels through the network channels (Chapter 19's
`backpressure{Upper,Lower}Threshold` settings) rather than
through the task queue. This is one of the cleaner consequences
of the decomposition strategy: a per-worker scheduler has no
global state to share, which is exactly what makes adding more
workers a question of "spin one up" rather than "reconfigure
the scheduler."

These are deliberate non-goals. The two-queue design is, by C++
standards of fanciness, almost embarrassingly modest. Two folly
queues. One semaphore. One stop token. About two hundred lines of
code, including tests. The lesson is not that the scheduler is small
because the problem is small. The lesson is that the scheduler is
small because the problems it does not solve are handled elsewhere —
the buffer manager handles memory pressure, the optimiser handles
operator placement, the source registry handles source-specific
backpressure. The scheduler does one thing: it gets work to workers
without deadlocking.

---

## Summary {#sec-summary}

A bounded shared task queue is the natural starting point for a
scheduler in a stream processing engine, but it leaves you with two
deadlock surfaces: worker-emission deadlock (P1) and source-flooding
deadlock (P2).

NebulaStream solves them with a structural separation: two queues,
each with different blocking semantics. The internal queue is
unbounded and never blocks a worker on emit, eliminating P1. The
admission queue is bounded and blocks producers, providing the
backpressure that keeps the engine from running out of memory while
preventing source floods from starving worker emissions, eliminating
P2. The two queues are unified for the worker via a
`std::counting_semaphore` whose count is the engine's authoritative
notion of "work available."

Cancellation is layered on top of both blocking calls via a 100 ms
poll on a `std::stop_token`, which gives shutdown a bounded latency
without measurable steady-state cost.

A subtle third failure mode — a self-emitting `PendingPipelineStopTask`
that monopolises the internal queue — is handled by a small backoff
mechanism that routes the task through a `DelayedTaskSubmitter`
after two failed attempts, ensuring source-emitted work in the
admission queue gets a chance to advance.

The design is deliberately minimal. Per-task prioritisation, per-pipeline
backpressure, and work stealing are all deferred to other parts of the
engine or to future work. What is left is small, fast, and — most
important — provably free of the two deadlock surfaces that motivated
its existence.

## Reading exercises {#sec-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 15.1: invariant under load"}
Run `TaskQueueTest`'s multi-producer/multi-consumer fuzzer:

```shell
ctest --test-dir cmake-build-debug -R "TaskQueueTest" \
    --output-on-failure
```

Read `nes-query-engine/tests/TaskQueueTest.cpp`. The test uses
a synthetic `Task` of size 142 bytes. Modify the test to use a
task of size 16 bytes and another of size 4096 bytes. Does the
invariant `internal.size() + admission.size() >= tasksAvailable`
still hold under contention? Use ThreadSanitizer
(`-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` with `-DNES_USE_SANITIZER=thread`) and
look for any reported races.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 15.2: P1 simulation"}
Modify a copy of `TaskQueue.hpp` to make the internal queue
*bounded* (replace `folly::UMPMCQueue` with `folly::MPMCQueue<TaskType>`
of, say, capacity 16). Make `addInternalTaskNonBlocking` return
`bool` and have it fail when full. Run the existing test suite. How
many tests fail? What pattern do the failures show? You should not
attempt to make the code "work" — the goal is to feel the deadlock
that the unbounded design prevents.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 15.3: pending pipeline stop in flight"}
Run a multi-stream join systest with `ENGINE_LOG_TRACE` enabled
and grep for `Pipeline ... is still active: ... Seen for ...th
time` in the log. How often, in a typical join with multiple
input streams, is a `PendingPipelineStopTask` re-emitted before
the pipeline can be stopped? What does that number tell you
about the typical fan-out of the join probe?

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1 \
    -- --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER
```

Inspect the resulting log file under `cmake-build-debug/systest-run`.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 15.4: cancellation latency"}
Start `nes-single-node-worker` and submit a long-running query
via `nes-repl`:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/nes-single-node-worker/nes-single-node-worker
# in another terminal
cmake-build-debug/nes-frontend/apps/repl/nes-repl -s localhost:8080 \
    < a-long-query.sql
```

Send `SIGINT` to the worker. Measure the time between the signal
and process exit using `time`. Where does the delay come from?
Identify the wait that dominates the latency (hint: it is bounded
by `StopTokenCheckInterval` per blocked thread). What would you
have to change to bring it below 10 ms?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 15.5: replace the semaphore"}
The `TaskQueue` uses a `std::counting_semaphore` to coordinate
producers and consumers. Could you replace it with a condition
variable and a counter? Sketch the implementation. What invariants
become harder to maintain? What additional state do you need? Why
might the authors have preferred the semaphore?
:::

## References {#sec-references}

This chapter draws on:

- **NebulaStream design document.** *Task Queues in the Query Engine.*
  In-tree at `docs/technical/QueryEngine_TaskQueue.md`. The originator
  of the P1/P2 framing used throughout this chapter.

- **NebulaStream source.** Commit `cd3ef68c73`. Specifically:

  - `nes-query-engine/TaskQueue.hpp`
  - `nes-query-engine/Task.hpp`
  - `nes-query-engine/QueryEngine.cpp` (the worker loop and
    `PendingPipelineStop` handling around line 600)
  - `nes-query-engine/Callback.hpp`
  - `nes-query-engine/DelayedTaskSubmitter.hpp`
  - `nes-query-engine/tests/TaskQueueTest.cpp`

- **Folly.** F. Bachrach et al. *Folly: Facebook open-source library*.
  `folly::MPMCQueue` and `folly::UMPMCQueue` are the underlying queue
  primitives. See `https://github.com/facebook/folly`.

- **Flink network buffers.** F. Hueske and V. Kalavri.
  *Stream Processing with Apache Flink*, 1st ed. O'Reilly Media, 2019,
  ch. 9, "Implementing Streaming Data Pipelines."

- **Spark Structured Streaming graceful stop.** M. Armbrust et al.
  *Structured Streaming: A Declarative API for Real-Time Applications
  in Apache Spark.* SIGMOD 2018.

- **Differential and timely dataflow.** F. McSherry, M. Isard, D. Murray.
  *Differential Dataflow.* CIDR 2013. And: D. Murray, F. McSherry et al.
  *Naiad: A Timely Dataflow System.* SOSP 2013.

- **C++20 stop token.** ISO/IEC 14882:2020. The `std::stop_token` and
  `std::counting_semaphore` types are from
  `<stop_token>` and `<semaphore>` respectively.

- **Continuation-style scheduler design.** As proposed in
  NebulaStream's design document (above). Note that the technique was
  superseded by the unbounded internal queue in the current
  implementation; the technique remains relevant if the queue is
  ever rebounded.

- **Variant-based task representation.** N. Josuttis. *The C++ Standard
  Library*, 2nd ed. Addison-Wesley, 2012, ch. 5 ("Utilities") for the
  general mechanics of `std::variant` and `std::visit`.
